name: ls
plain: `ls` shows what is in a folder. Its many options change which files appear (including hidden ones), how much detail you see (permissions, owner, size, dates) and the order.
In security work the details matter: who owns a file, who can write it, when it changed and whether it is really a link.
when: Find the newest or biggest file.
Check for symbolic links, executables and odd owners.

options.plain: Show hidden files (names starting with a dot), including . and ..
Like -a but without . and ..
options.use: Hidden files without the two special entries.

options.plain: Long listing: permissions, links, owner, group, size, date and name.
With -l or -s, show sizes as 1K, 234M, 2G.
Like -h but use powers of 1000, not 1024.
Use 1024-byte blocks for sizes.
Scale sizes by SIZE (for example M or 1K).
options.use: Showing every size in the same unit.

options.plain: Print the allocated size of each file in blocks.
options.use: Seeing disk use rather than length.

options.plain: Sort by file size, largest first.
Sort by modification time, newest first.
With -t sort by access time; with -l show access time.
With -t sort by status-change time; with -l show it.
Choose which time to show or sort by: atime, ctime, birth, mtime.
Choose the time format: full-iso, long-iso, iso, locale or +FORMAT.
Same as -l --time-style=full-iso.
options.use: Full time with seconds and zone.

Sort by file extension.

Reverse the sort order.
Sort by none, size, time, version or extension (-S -t -v -X).
List directories before files.
List directories themselves, not their contents.
options.use: Checking a folder's own permissions: ls -ld /tmp.

options.plain: List sub-folders too.
One entry per line.
Choose the layout by name: across (-x), commas (-m), horizontal (-x), long (-l), single-column (-1), verbose (-l), vertical (-C).
-C columns down, -x columns across, -m comma-separated, -g like -l without the owner, -o like -l without the group.
Show numeric owner and group ids.

With -l print the author of each file.

options.plain: Print the inode number of each file.
Add a mark to each name: / folder, * executable, @ link, = socket, | pipe. -p adds only the slash; --file-type skips the star.
options.use: Telling types apart at a glance.

options.plain: Colour the output (always, auto, never) / make file names clickable in some terminals.

options.plain: Show information about the target of symbolic links instead of the link, or only for names given on the command line.
How to print names with spaces and odd characters: escaped, literal, in quotes or in a chosen style.
Print ? instead of control characters / print them as they are.
Output width / tab stops.
options.use: Fitting the output to your screen.

options.plain: Skip files that match a pattern, files ending in ~, or hide patterns unless -a is used.
-D prints for Emacs; -Z shows the security (SELinux) label; --zero ends lines with NUL.
Print a short usage message / the version and exit.

mistakes: Forgetting -a: hidden files (.env, .ssh, .bash_history) will not show.
ls -l on a folder shows its contents; use -d to see the folder itself.
Parsing ls output in scripts: use find or shell globs, because names can contain spaces and newlines.
Reading the permission string wrongly: the first character is the type (- file, d folder, l link), then three triplets: owner, group, others.
try: Find the three biggest files in /usr/bin with ls -lS.
Find the file in a folder that changed most recently.
Read the permissions of /tmp and /etc/passwd and explain each letter.
Create a hard link and a symbolic link and tell them apart with ls -li.
